subject: Biology
title: Neural Control and Coordination
summary: How the body coordinates itself through the neural system: the divisions of the human neural system, the neuron and its types, how a nerve impulse is generated by ion movements and conducted along an axon, how it crosses a synapse, the three parts of the brain with their functions, and the reflex arc. It is the base for Class 12 Chemical Coordination and for a reliable one or two NEET questions every year, and it is one of the most diagram-driven chapters in Class 11 Zoology.

exam_profile.weightage: Class 11 Biology is a 70-mark theory paper set by the school on the CBSE pattern. Neural Control and Coordination sits in Unit V, Human Physiology, the largest unit of the paper (roughly 18 to 20 marks shared among Breathing and Exchange of Gases, Body Fluids and Circulation, Excretory Products, Locomotion and Movement, Neural Control and Chemical Coordination). In a typical school final this chapter gives 5 to 8 marks: one or two 1-mark items (an MCQ on Nissl's granules, the sodium-potassium pump, the site of bipolar neurons, corpora quadrigemina, the meninges or the medulla, and an Assertion-Reason on myelinated conduction or grey matter), a 2-mark or 3-mark question on the types of neurons, chemical versus electrical synapse, myelinated versus non-myelinated fibres, or the functions of a named brain part, and most years a 5-mark question that pairs a labelled diagram with the mechanism of impulse generation and conduction, synaptic transmission, or the structure of the brain. NEET reliably takes one or two questions straight from the NCERT figures and wording. Under the rationalised syllabus the sense organs (eye and ear) are removed, so the whole weight falls on the neuron, the impulse, the synapse, the brain and the reflex arc.

question_types.note: Where Nissl's granules are found (cell body and dendrites); where neurotransmitters are stored (synaptic vesicles of the synaptic knob); the sodium-potassium pump ratio (3 Na<sup>+</sup> out, 2 K<sup>+</sup> in); which ion the resting membrane is more permeable to (K<sup>+</sup>); which ion rushes in during depolarisation (Na<sup>+</sup>); the site of multipolar (cerebral cortex), bipolar (retina) and unipolar (embryonic stage) neurons; nodes of Ranvier; which nerves are myelinated (cranial and spinal); the three meninges in order; corpus callosum; corpora quadrigemina in the midbrain; cerebral aqueduct; the centres in the medulla (respiration, cardiovascular reflexes, gastric secretions); the hypothalamus as the master clock; the limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus); the parts of the brain stem; the dorsal root carrying afferent fibres.

Conduction is faster in myelinated fibres because depolarisation happens only at the nodes of Ranvier; the cerebral cortex is grey matter because of the concentration of neuron cell bodies; electrical synapses are faster but rare in our body; the inside of a resting axon is negative because the membrane is nearly impermeable to Na<sup>+</sup> and the negatively charged proteins stay inside; a reflex is involuntary yet involves the spinal cord; a chemical synapse can be excitatory or inhibitory depending on the ion channels opened; the cerebellum is highly convoluted to accommodate more neurons.

Define coordination, synapse, action potential, resting potential, reflex action, reflex arc, nodes of Ranvier; name the three meninges; name the parts of the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain; two functions of the hypothalamus or the medulla; distinguish afferent and efferent neurons, dendrite and axon, grey and white matter; what forms the brain stem; which part of the brain is most developed and which acts as the master clock; why is the Na<sup>+</sup>–K<sup>+</sup> pump needed; name the neurotransmitter-containing structure at the axon terminal.

The three types of neurons with location; myelinated versus non-myelinated fibres; chemical versus electrical synapse; the steps of synaptic transmission; the role of Na<sup>+</sup> in the generation of the action potential; polarisation and depolarisation; the divisions of the human neural system as a flow chart; thalamus versus hypothalamus; cerebrum versus cerebellum; cranial versus spinal nerves; the components of a reflex arc; functions of the hindbrain parts; the limbic system.

Labelled diagram of a neuron plus its types and the myelinated/non-myelinated distinction; generation and conduction of a nerve impulse with the NCERT site-A/site-B diagram (the most repeated 5-marker); the mechanism of synaptic transmission with a labelled synapse; the sagittal section of the human brain with the functions of forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain; the reflex arc with the knee-jerk diagram and the sequence receptor → afferent → CNS → efferent → effector.

A passage on the knee-jerk test in a clinic (receptor, dorsal root ganglion, interneuron, ventral root, effector); a passage on a local anaesthetic or toxin that blocks Na<sup>+</sup> channels (no depolarisation, no action potential); a passage on a patient with a hindbrain injury (loss of balance, irregular breathing and heart rate); a passage on the ion table across the resting membrane; a passage on a poison that stops neurotransmitter release or blocks the post-synaptic receptor.

hot_topics: Generation and conduction of the nerve impulse: resting potential, the Na<sup>+</sup>–K<sup>+</sup> pump (3 out, 2 in), depolarisation by Na<sup>+</sup> influx, repolarisation by K<sup>+</sup> efflux, and the current loop between sites A and B
Synaptic transmission: chemical synapse steps (vesicle movement, fusion, release, receptor binding, ion channel opening) and the chemical versus electrical comparison
Structure of a neuron with the labelled NCERT diagram; multipolar, bipolar and unipolar neurons; myelinated versus non-myelinated axons and the nodes of Ranvier
Sagittal section of the human brain: forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus), midbrain (cerebral aqueduct, corpora quadrigemina), hindbrain (pons, cerebellum, medulla) with one function each
Reflex action and reflex arc: the knee-jerk diagram with receptor, afferent neuron, dorsal root ganglion, interneuron, efferent neuron, ventral root, effector
Divisions of the human neural system: CNS and PNS; afferent and efferent fibres; somatic and autonomic; sympathetic and parasympathetic; the visceral nervous system
The meninges (dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater), grey matter versus white matter, corpus callosum, cerebral cortex and its motor, sensory and association areas
Named comparisons: dendrite vs axon, thalamus vs hypothalamus, cerebrum vs cerebellum, afferent vs efferent, cranial vs spinal nerves

sections.heading: 18.1 Neural System: why coordination is needed and how it is provided
sections.body:
NCERT opens the chapter with a simple point. When you run, your legs work harder, so your muscles need more oxygen and glucose. To supply them the heart beats faster, the breathing rate rises, the blood vessels to the muscles widen and the liver releases glucose. Several organs are changing what they do at the same time, in the right direction, and they fall back to normal when you stop. This is what NCERT calls coordination: the process through which two or more organs interact and complement each other's functions. In humans two systems do this job together. The neural system provides an organised network of point-to-point connections, so its control is quick and precise. The endocrine system provides chemical integration through hormones, which is slower but longer-lasting. This chapter is about the first one; the next chapter is about the second.

The neural system of all animals is made of highly specialised cells called neurons, which can detect, receive and transmit different kinds of stimuli. How elaborate the system is depends on how complex the animal is. In Hydra the neural organisation is very simple: a diffuse network of neurons with no brain. In insects the system is better organised: there is a brain together with a number of ganglia and neural tissues. Vertebrates have a more developed neural system with a large, well-protected brain, a spinal cord and a full set of nerves. The examiner expects you to be able to quote these three examples in the same order as NCERT and to be able to define coordination in one sentence.

Keep the contrast between neural and hormonal control in mind because a short question often asks for it: neural control is fast, point-to-point, and its effect stops when the impulse stops; hormonal control is slower, reaches every cell that the blood reaches, and its effect lasts as long as the hormone stays in circulation. Both are needed, and the hypothalamus of the brain is the place where the two systems meet.

formulas.expr: Coordination = two or more organs interacting and complementing each other's functions
where: point-to-point network of neurons, rapid coordination
hormones carried by blood, chemical integration

sections.tip: If asked why the neural system gives faster coordination than the endocrine system, write two marking points: it works through a network of point-to-point connections, and its signal is an electrical impulse rather than a chemical carried by the blood.

sections.heading: 18.2 Human Neural System: CNS, PNS, somatic and autonomic divisions
sections.body:
The human neural system is divided into two parts. The central neural system (CNS) includes the brain and the spinal cord and is the site of information processing and control. The peripheral neural system (PNS) comprises all the nerves of the body associated with the CNS. The nerve fibres of the PNS are of two types. Afferent fibres transmit impulses from tissues and organs to the CNS; efferent fibres transmit regulatory impulses from the CNS to the concerned peripheral tissues and organs. A simple memory aid: afferent arrives at the CNS, efferent exits it.

The PNS is further divided into two divisions on the basis of what it controls. The somatic neural system relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles, so it handles voluntary actions. The autonomic neural system transmits impulses from the CNS to the involuntary organs and smooth muscles of the body, such as the heart, the gut and the glands. The autonomic system is itself divided into the sympathetic neural system and the parasympathetic neural system. NCERT does not list their individual actions in this chapter, but a school paper may expect the general idea: the two usually act in opposite directions on the same organ, the sympathetic division preparing the body for activity and the parasympathetic division restoring the resting state.

NCERT also names the visceral nervous system: it is the part of the peripheral neural system that comprises the whole complex of nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses by which impulses travel from the CNS to the viscera and from the viscera to the CNS. In practice this term overlaps with the autonomic system, and it is asked as a one-line definition.

Two numbers are not printed in the rationalised NCERT text but are so commonly asked in school papers that you should know them: humans have 12 pairs of cranial nerves, which arise from the brain, and 31 pairs of spinal nerves, which arise from the spinal cord. Cranial nerves may be sensory, motor or mixed; every spinal nerve is mixed, formed by the joining of a dorsal (sensory) root and a ventral (motor) root. Practise drawing the whole division as a flow chart: Neural system → CNS (brain, spinal cord) and PNS → afferent and efferent fibres → somatic and autonomic → sympathetic and parasympathetic. A 3-mark question often asks for exactly that chart.

formulas.expr: Neural system → CNS (brain + spinal cord) + PNS (all nerves) → PNS: somatic (voluntary, skeletal muscle) + autonomic (involuntary organs) → autonomic: sympathetic + parasympathetic
where: carries impulses from tissues and organs to the CNS
carries impulses from the CNS to peripheral tissues and organs

formulas.expr: 12 pairs of cranial nerves (from the brain); 31 pairs of spinal nerves (from the spinal cord)
where: mixed nerve formed by the dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots

sections.tip: Students mix up 'somatic' and 'sympathetic'. Somatic is a division of the PNS controlling skeletal muscle; sympathetic is a division of the autonomic system. Write the flow chart and the confusion disappears.

sections.heading: 18.3 Neuron as the structural and functional unit: structure, types, myelinated and non-myelinated fibres
sections.body:
A neuron is a microscopic structure composed of three major parts: the cell body, the dendrites and the axon. The cell body (cyton) contains cytoplasm with the typical cell organelles and, in addition, certain granular bodies called Nissl's granules. Short fibres that branch repeatedly and project out of the cell body are the dendrites; they also contain Nissl's granules and they transmit impulses towards the cell body. The axon is a long fibre whose distal end is branched; each branch terminates as a bulb-like structure called the synaptic knob, which possesses synaptic vesicles containing chemicals called neurotransmitters. Axons transmit nerve impulses away from the cell body to a synapse or to a neuro-muscular junction. In the NCERT figure the labels to learn are dendrite, cell body, nucleus, Nissl's granules, axon, Schwann cell, myelin sheath, node of Ranvier and axon terminal.

Types of neurons. Based on the number of axons and dendrites, neurons are divided into three types. Multipolar neurons have one axon and two or more dendrites and are found in the cerebral cortex. Bipolar neurons have one axon and one dendrite and are found in the retina of the eye. Unipolar neurons have a cell body with one axon only and are usually found in the embryonic stage. The location is the part the examiner checks, so learn the three pairs together: multipolar–cerebral cortex, bipolar–retina, unipolar–embryo.

Myelinated and non-myelinated fibres. There are two types of axons. The myelinated nerve fibres are enveloped by Schwann cells, which form a myelin sheath around the axon; the gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths are called nodes of Ranvier. Myelinated nerve fibres are found in spinal and cranial nerves. In non-myelinated (unmyelinated) fibres the axon is enclosed by a Schwann cell that does not form a myelin sheath around it, and such fibres are commonly found in the autonomous and the somatic neural systems. The functional difference matters for the next section: in a myelinated fibre the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), so conduction is much faster than in a non-myelinated fibre where the whole membrane has to depolarise in turn.

A neuron is described as the structural and functional unit of the neural system because it is the cell that actually receives the stimulus (at the dendrites), conducts it (along the axon) and hands it on (at the synaptic knob). Every other structure in the chapter, from a nerve to the cerebral cortex, is built out of neurons and their supporting cells.

formulas.expr: Neuron = cell body (cyton, with Nissl's granules) + dendrites (towards the cell body) + axon (away from the cell body, ends in synaptic knobs with synaptic vesicles)
where: granular bodies present in the cell body and the dendrites, absent from the axon
bulb-like end of each axon branch holding vesicles of neurotransmitter

formulas.expr: Multipolar: 1 axon + ≥2 dendrites (cerebral cortex); Bipolar: 1 axon + 1 dendrite (retina); Unipolar: cell body + 1 axon (embryonic stage)
where: Schwann cells form a myelin sheath; nodes of Ranvier between sheaths; spinal and cranial nerves
Schwann cell present but no myelin sheath; autonomous and somatic neural systems

sections.tip: In the neuron diagram the Schwann cell and the myelin sheath must be labelled separately, and the node of Ranvier is the gap, not a swelling. A neuron drawn without the synaptic knobs at the axon terminal usually loses a label mark.

sections.heading: 18.3.1 Generation of the nerve impulse: the polarised resting membrane and the Na⁺–K⁺ pump
sections.body:
Neurons are excitable cells: their membranes are in a polarised state. To understand why, look at the axonal membrane. It carries different types of ion channels, and each channel is selectively permeable to a particular ion. When a neuron is not conducting any impulse, that is, when it is resting, the axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to potassium ions (K+) and nearly impermeable to sodium ions (Na+). It is also impermeable to the negatively charged proteins present in the axoplasm. As a result the axoplasm inside the axon contains a high concentration of K+ and of negatively charged proteins and a low concentration of Na+, while the fluid outside the axon contains a low concentration of K+ and a high concentration of Na+. So there is a concentration gradient across the membrane for each ion.

These ionic gradients would run down by diffusion if nothing maintained them. They are maintained by the active transport of ions by the sodium–potassium pump, which transports 3 Na+ outwards for 2 K+ into the cell, using ATP. Because the pump pushes out three positive charges for every two it brings in, and because K+ keeps leaking out through the K+ channels while the negative proteins stay trapped inside, the outer surface of the membrane becomes positively charged and the inner surface negatively charged. The membrane is then said to be polarised, and the electrical potential difference across the resting plasma membrane is called the resting potential. NCERT does not give a value; the usual figure quoted is about −70 mV (inside negative relative to outside), and you may write it as an extra point but not in place of the explanation.

When the exercise asks you to explain the polarisation of the membrane of a nerve fibre, the marking scheme looks for four points in order: (1) unequal permeability, more to K+, nearly none to Na+, none to the negative proteins; (2) the resulting distribution, K+ and proteins high inside, Na+ high outside; (3) the Na+–K+ pump, 3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in, maintaining the gradient by active transport; (4) the conclusion, outer surface positive, inner surface negative, resting potential. Write them as four numbered lines and you will not miss a mark.

formulas.expr: Resting membrane: more permeable to K<sup>+</sup>, nearly impermeable to Na<sup>+</sup>, impermeable to negatively charged proteins
where: high K<sup>+</sup>, high negatively charged proteins, low Na<sup>+</sup>

formulas.expr: Na<sup>+</sup>–K<sup>+</sup> pump: 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out : 2 K<sup>+</sup> in per cycle (active transport, uses ATP)
where: electrical potential difference across the resting membrane; outside positive, inside negative; about −70 mV (value not in NCERT)

sections.tip: The ratio is always 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out and 2 K<sup>+</sup> in. A MCQ that reverses the numbers or the directions is a standard trap.

sections.heading: 18.3.1 Action potential and conduction of the impulse along the axon
sections.body:
Now apply a stimulus to the axon at a site, call it site A, as in NCERT Fig. 18.2. The membrane at site A becomes freely permeable to Na+. This leads to a rapid influx of Na+, followed by a reversal of the polarity at that site: the outer surface of the membrane becomes negatively charged and the inner side becomes positively charged. The polarity of the membrane at site A is thus reversed and the membrane is said to be depolarised. The electrical potential difference across the plasma membrane at site A is now called the action potential, which is in fact the nerve impulse. So the marking points for 'depolarisation' are: stimulus → membrane freely permeable to Na+ → rapid Na+ influx → polarity reversed, inside positive and outside negative → action potential.

How does the impulse move? At the site immediately ahead, site B, the membrane is still at rest, so its outer surface is positive and its inner surface is negative. Because site A now has the opposite polarity, a current flows on the inner surface from site A to site B, and on the outer surface a current flows from site B to site A, completing the circuit of current flow. This local current reverses the polarity at site B: an action potential is generated at site B. The action potential, that is the impulse, generated at site A thus arrives at site B. The sequence is repeated along the length of the axon and in this way the impulse is conducted. Draw the two sites with their charges and the two arrows of current when you answer 'conduction of a nerve impulse along a nerve fibre'; the figure carries marks.

What happens back at site A? The rise in the stimulus-induced permeability to Na+ is extremely short-lived. It is quickly followed by a rise in the permeability to K+. Within a fraction of a second K+ diffuses outside the membrane and restores the resting potential of the membrane at the site of excitation, and the fibre becomes once more responsive to further stimulation. This restoration is called repolarisation, and the Na+–K+ pump then slowly restores the original ion distribution. The action potential is therefore a brief event: Na+ in (depolarisation, rising phase), K+ out (repolarisation, falling phase), pump resets. In a myelinated fibre the same events occur only at the nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse leaps from node to node and travels much faster; this is what the exercise wants when it asks you to distinguish conduction in myelinated and unmyelinated fibres.

Two consequences are worth stating in an answer. First, the action potential is all-or-none: a stimulus either reaches threshold and produces a full impulse or produces none. Second, the impulse travels in one direction along the axon under normal conditions because the region just behind is still recovering. Neither is stated in NCERT in those words, so use them as supporting sentences rather than as the core of the answer.

formulas.expr: Stimulus at site A → membrane freely permeable to Na<sup>+</sup> → Na<sup>+</sup> influx → inside positive, outside negative (depolarised) → action potential = nerve impulse
where: the potential difference across the membrane at the depolarised site; usually about +30 mV inside (value not in NCERT)

formulas.expr: Current on inner surface: A → B; current on outer surface: B → A → polarity at B reversed → action potential at B → repeated along the axon
where: short-lived Na<sup>+</sup> permeability followed by rise in K<sup>+</sup> permeability; K<sup>+</sup> diffuses out and restores the resting potential

sections.tip: Write the direction of both currents. 'Inner surface from A to B, outer surface from B to A' is the sentence examiners underline; a single arrow earns half the mark.

sections.heading: 18.3.2 Transmission of impulses across a synapse: electrical and chemical synapses
sections.body:
A nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to another through junctions called synapses. A synapse is formed by the membranes of a pre-synaptic neuron and a post-synaptic neuron, which may or may not be separated by a gap called the synaptic cleft. That single sentence of NCERT is the definition to write when 'synapse' is asked as a short note, and it leads straight to the two kinds of synapse.

At an electrical synapse the membranes of the pre- and post-synaptic neurons are in very close proximity. Electrical current can flow directly from one neuron into the other across the synapse, so transmission is very similar to impulse conduction along a single axon. Impulse transmission across an electrical synapse is always faster than that across a chemical synapse, but electrical synapses are rare in our system. Three comparison points: no cleft (or almost none), no neurotransmitter, faster but rare.

At a chemical synapse the membranes of the pre- and post-synaptic neurons are separated by a fluid-filled space, the synaptic cleft. Chemicals called neurotransmitters are involved in the transmission of impulses at these synapses. The axon terminals contain vesicles filled with these neurotransmitters. NCERT gives the mechanism in a clear sequence, and the 3-mark or 5-mark question on 'mechanism of synaptic transmission' expects each step: (1) when an impulse (action potential) arrives at the axon terminal, it stimulates the movement of the synaptic vesicles towards the membrane; (2) the vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and release their neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft; (3) the released neurotransmitters bind to their specific receptors present on the post-synaptic membrane; (4) this binding opens ion channels, allowing the entry of ions which can generate a new potential in the post-synaptic neuron. The new potential developed may be either excitatory or inhibitory, depending on which ion channels are opened. The labelled figure has the axon terminal, synaptic vesicles, synaptic cleft, neurotransmitters, receptors and the post-synaptic membrane.

NCERT does not name individual neurotransmitters in this chapter, but acetylcholine is the one usually quoted in school papers as the transmitter at the neuro-muscular junction (it appears in the Locomotion chapter). Note also that the transmission at a chemical synapse is one-way: only the pre-synaptic knob has vesicles and only the post-synaptic membrane has the receptors. Because the transmitter must diffuse across the cleft, chemical transmission introduces a short synaptic delay, which is the reason an electrical synapse is faster.

formulas.expr: Synapse = membranes of a pre-synaptic neuron and a post-synaptic neuron, with or without a synaptic cleft
where: membranes very close; current flows directly; faster; rare in our system
separated by a synaptic cleft; uses neurotransmitters from synaptic vesicles

formulas.expr: Chemical transmission: impulse at axon terminal → vesicles move to membrane → fuse and release neurotransmitter into cleft → binds specific receptors on post-synaptic membrane → ion channels open → new potential (excitatory or inhibitory)
where: the new potential brings the post-synaptic neuron nearer to firing an impulse
the new potential makes the post-synaptic neuron less likely to fire

sections.tip: The most common lost mark: writing 'the impulse crosses the synapse'. It does not. The impulse stops at the pre-synaptic knob; a chemical crosses the cleft and a new impulse is generated on the other side.

sections.heading: 18.4 Central Neural System: the brain, its functions and its protective coverings
sections.body:
The brain is the central information processing organ of our body and acts as the command and control system. NCERT gives a list of what it controls, and a 2-mark question can ask for any four of them: the voluntary movements, the balance of the body, the functioning of vital involuntary organs such as the lungs, heart and kidneys, thermoregulation, hunger and thirst, circadian (24-hour) rhythms of our body, the activities of several endocrine glands, and human behaviour. It is also the site for the processing of vision, hearing, speech, memory, intelligence, emotions and thoughts.

The human brain is well protected by the skull. Inside the skull the brain is covered by three cranial meninges. From outside inward they are the dura mater, the outer thick layer; the arachnoid, a very thin middle layer; and the pia mater, the inner layer which is in contact with the brain tissue. The order is asked as an MCQ almost every year, so learn it as D-A-P from outside to inside. The space between the arachnoid and the pia mater holds the cerebrospinal fluid, which cushions the brain; the same fluid fills the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord. That detail is from the exemplar rather than the main text, but it turns up in MCQs.

The brain can be divided into three major parts: the forebrain, the midbrain and the hindbrain. The forebrain consists of the cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus. The midbrain lies between the forebrain and the hindbrain. The hindbrain consists of the pons, cerebellum and medulla oblongata. The midbrain and hindbrain together form the brain stem, which continues below as the spinal cord. When the examiner asks you to 'briefly describe the structure of the brain', open with the meninges, then the three parts in this order, then the parts of each, and finish with the brain stem. The next three sections give you the content for each part.

The spinal cord is the other component of the CNS. It runs down the vertebral canal, is covered by the same three meninges and has grey matter in the centre (in the shape of a butterfly or an H) surrounded by white matter, the reverse of the arrangement in the cerebrum. It carries impulses to and from the brain and is the centre for spinal reflexes, which is where it reappears in section 18.5.

formulas.expr: Meninges (outside → inside): dura mater (thick outer) → arachnoid (thin middle) → pia mater (inner, touches the brain)
where: midbrain + hindbrain (pons and medulla); continues as the spinal cord

formulas.expr: Brain = forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus) + midbrain + hindbrain (pons, cerebellum, medulla oblongata)
where: voluntary movements, balance, vital involuntary organs, thermoregulation, hunger, thirst, circadian rhythms, endocrine glands, behaviour; vision, hearing, speech, memory, intelligence, emotions, thoughts

sections.tip: For 'name the protective structures of the brain' write both the skull and the three meninges in order. Students who write only 'meninges' get one mark out of two.

sections.heading: 18.4.1 Forebrain: cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus and the limbic system
sections.body:
The cerebrum forms the major part of the human brain. A deep cleft, the longitudinal fissure, divides the cerebrum longitudinally into two halves, the left and right cerebral hemispheres. The hemispheres are connected by a tract of nerve fibres called the corpus callosum. The layer of cells which covers each cerebral hemisphere is called the cerebral cortex, and it is thrown into prominent folds, which increase its surface area. The cerebral cortex is referred to as the grey matter because of its greyish appearance, which is due to the concentration of neuron cell bodies there. The cortex contains motor areas, sensory areas and large regions that are neither clearly sensory nor motor in function. These regions are called association areas and are responsible for complex functions like intersensory associations, memory and communication. Beneath the cortex, the fibres of the tracts are covered with the myelin sheath; they constitute the inner part of the cerebral hemisphere and give it an opaque white appearance, hence white matter. So in the cerebrum grey matter is outside and white matter inside, while in the spinal cord it is the reverse.

The cerebrum wraps around a structure called the thalamus, which is a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling. Almost every sensory input on its way to the cortex is relayed through the thalamus. Lying at the base of the thalamus is the hypothalamus. It contains a number of centres which control the urge for eating and drinking and the body temperature. It also contains several groups of neurosecretory cells, which secrete hormones; this is how the neural and endocrine systems are linked, and it is why the hypothalamus is called the master clock of the body (it sets the circadian rhythm) and the controller of the pituitary in the next chapter. When the exercise asks which part of the central neural system acts as a master clock, the answer is the hypothalamus.

The inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres and a group of associated deep structures like the amygdala and the hippocampus form a complex structure called the limbic lobe or limbic system. Along with the hypothalamus it is involved in the regulation of sexual behaviour, the expression of emotional reactions (for example excitement, pleasure, rage and fear) and motivation. Which part of the human brain is the most developed? The cerebrum, specifically its cerebral cortex, which is the seat of intelligence, memory, reasoning and speech.

Two comparison questions come from this section. Thalamus versus hypothalamus: the thalamus is a relay and coordinating centre for sensory and motor signals; the hypothalamus lies below it, houses the centres for hunger, thirst and temperature and produces hormones through neurosecretory cells. Cerebrum versus cerebellum: the cerebrum is the largest part, in the forebrain, with grey matter outside and association areas for memory and intelligence; the cerebellum is in the hindbrain, controls balance and posture and the coordination of voluntary movements, and has a highly convoluted surface.

formulas.expr: Cerebrum: longitudinal fissure → two cerebral hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum; cortex = grey matter (cell bodies) with motor, sensory and association areas; inner myelinated tracts = white matter
where: tract of nerve fibres connecting the two hemispheres

formulas.expr: Thalamus = coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling; Hypothalamus = centres for eating, drinking, body temperature + neurosecretory cells (hormones); Limbic system = inner hemispheres + amygdala + hippocampus → sexual behaviour, emotions, motivation

sections.tip: Grey matter is grey because of cell bodies; white matter is white because of myelinated fibres. Give the reason with the colour whenever the question carries 2 marks.

sections.heading: 18.4.2 Midbrain: cerebral aqueduct and corpora quadrigemina
sections.body:
The midbrain is the smallest of the three divisions and NCERT gives it three sentences, but each one is an examination fact. It is located between the thalamus and hypothalamus of the forebrain and the pons of the hindbrain. A canal called the cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain; it connects the third ventricle of the forebrain with the fourth ventricle of the hindbrain and carries cerebrospinal fluid. The dorsal portion of the midbrain consists mainly of four round swellings, called lobes, known as the corpora quadrigemina. The word means 'four bodies': the upper pair (superior colliculi) is concerned with visual reflexes and the lower pair (inferior colliculi) with auditory reflexes, though NCERT only asks you to know the name and position. The ventral part of the midbrain contains the crura cerebri (cerebral peduncles), the bundles of fibres connecting the forebrain to the hindbrain; this label appears in many school diagrams although it is not in the rationalised text.

The midbrain and the hindbrain together form the brain stem. Remember that the brain stem is the part that is continuous with the spinal cord and that all the fibre tracts between the cerebrum and the body pass through it, so an injury there is far more dangerous than an injury to the cortex of a similar size.

For the short note on the midbrain, which is exercise 5(c), the marking points are: position (between forebrain and pons), the cerebral aqueduct, the corpora quadrigemina on the dorsal side, and its membership of the brain stem. Four lines, four marks' worth of content, and a small labelled sketch of the sagittal section with the midbrain shaded will make the answer complete.

formulas.expr: Midbrain: between thalamus/hypothalamus (forebrain) and pons (hindbrain); cerebral aqueduct passes through it; dorsal side = corpora quadrigemina (four round swellings)
where: four lobes on the dorsal midbrain; upper pair visual reflexes, lower pair auditory reflexes (extra detail)

sections.tip: Corpora quadrigemina belongs to the midbrain, not the hindbrain, and it is 'four' round swellings, not two. Both are MCQ traps.

sections.heading: 18.4.3 Hindbrain: pons, cerebellum and medulla oblongata
sections.body:
The hindbrain comprises the pons, the cerebellum and the medulla (also called the medulla oblongata). The pons consists of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain; it lies in front of the cerebellum and above the medulla and acts as a bridge (that is what 'pons' means) between the cerebellum, the cerebrum and the medulla. It also contains centres that help the medulla regulate breathing, which is how many school papers phrase its function.

The cerebellum has a very convoluted surface in order to provide additional space for many more neurons. Functionally, the cerebellum coordinates voluntary movements and maintains the posture and balance (equilibrium) of the body. This is the answer to the popular question 'which part of the nervous system is responsible for maintaining balance and coordination of body movements?' A person with cerebellar damage can still move but moves clumsily and cannot stand steadily.

The medulla of the brain is connected to the spinal cord. It contains centres which control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions. Because the centres for breathing and for heart rate sit here, the medulla is the most vital part of the brain: injury to it is fatal even when the rest of the brain is intact. Together with the midbrain, the pons and the medulla form the brain stem.

Exercise 5(d) asks for a short note on the hindbrain and exercise 8(d) asks for cerebrum versus cerebellum. For the short note write three lines, one for each part with its function. For the difference, place the two side by side: cerebrum (forebrain, largest part, grey matter outside, seat of intelligence, memory, voluntary control) against cerebellum (hindbrain, second largest part, convoluted surface, balance, posture and coordination of movement). A helpful way to keep the hindbrain functions straight is to ask what stops working when the part is damaged: cerebellum, you fall over; medulla, you stop breathing; pons, the traffic between the parts of the brain is cut.

formulas.expr: Pons = fibre tracts interconnecting regions of the brain; Cerebellum = very convoluted surface, more neurons, balance and coordination of movement; Medulla = connected to spinal cord, centres for respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions
where: the vital centre of the brain; continues as the spinal cord
second largest part of the brain

sections.tip: Three functions of the medulla, quoted in NCERT order: respiration, cardiovascular reflexes, gastric secretions. Writing 'controls involuntary functions' without naming them gets half marks.

sections.heading: 18.5 Reflex Action and Reflex Arc
sections.body:
You must have experienced a sudden withdrawal of a body part which comes in contact with something that is extremely hot, cold, pointed or an animal that is scary. The entire process of response to a peripheral nervous stimulation that occurs involuntarily, that is without conscious effort or thought, and requires the involvement of a part of the central neural system, is called a reflex action. That is the NCERT definition and it has three parts the examiner looks for: a response to a peripheral stimulus, involuntary, and involving a part of the CNS (usually the spinal cord). The last part is what students forget; a reflex is involuntary but it is not independent of the CNS.

The reflex pathway comprises at least one afferent neuron (receptor) and one efferent neuron (effector or excitor) appropriately arranged in a series. The afferent neuron receives the signal from a sensory organ and transmits the impulse via the dorsal nerve root into the CNS, at the level of the spinal cord. The efferent neuron then carries the signal from the CNS to the effector, leaving through the ventral nerve root. The stimulus and the response thus form a reflex arc. In many reflexes an interneuron (association neuron) inside the grey matter of the spinal cord connects the afferent and efferent neurons; in the simplest reflexes, such as the knee jerk, the afferent neuron synapses directly with the efferent neuron.

NCERT Fig. 18.5 shows the knee-jerk reflex, and this is the diagram to practise. A tap below the kneecap stretches the thigh muscle; the receptor (muscle spindle) in the muscle generates impulses; the sensory (afferent) neuron, whose cell body lies in the dorsal root ganglion, carries them through the dorsal root into the spinal cord; there the signal passes (directly or through an interneuron) to the motor (efferent) neuron whose cell body lies in the grey matter; the motor neuron's axon leaves through the ventral root and reaches the effector, the thigh muscle, which contracts and the leg kicks. Write the sequence receptor → afferent neuron → dorsal root → spinal cord (integrating centre) → efferent neuron → ventral root → effector.

Why do reflexes exist? Because the pathway is short and does not wait for the brain, the response is faster than a conscious action and protects the body from damage. The brain is informed afterwards, which is why you feel the pain of the hot pan a moment after your hand has already moved. Distinguish a reflex from a voluntary action in a 2-mark answer: reflex, involuntary, spinal cord as the centre, very fast, stereotyped; voluntary, conscious, cerebrum involved, slower, variable.

formulas.expr: Reflex action = involuntary response to a peripheral stimulus that involves a part of the CNS; Reflex arc = receptor → afferent neuron (dorsal root) → CNS (spinal cord, interneuron) → efferent neuron (ventral root) → effector
where: cluster of cell bodies of the afferent (sensory) neurons on the dorsal root
muscle or gland that produces the response

sections.tip: In the reflex arc diagram the afferent neuron must enter through the dorsal root with its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion, and the efferent neuron must leave through the ventral root. Swapping dorsal and ventral is the commonest diagram error in this chapter.

key_terms.definition: The process through which two or more organs interact and complement each other's functions, so that the body responds to a change as one unit.
The brain and the spinal cord; the site of information processing and control.
All the nerves of the body associated with the CNS; it has afferent fibres carrying impulses to the CNS and efferent fibres carrying impulses from the CNS.

The two divisions of the PNS. The somatic system relays impulses from the CNS to skeletal muscles (voluntary); the autonomic system relays impulses from the CNS to involuntary organs and smooth muscles and is subdivided into sympathetic and parasympathetic systems.
The part of the PNS comprising the whole complex of nerves, fibres, ganglia and plexuses by which impulses travel from the CNS to the viscera and from the viscera to the CNS.
The structural and functional unit of the neural system, made of a cell body, dendrites and an axon; a highly specialised cell that can detect, receive and transmit stimuli.
Granular bodies present in the cytoplasm of the cell body and the dendrites of a neuron (absent from the axon).
The bulb-like terminal of each axon branch, containing synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitter.

key_terms.term: Myelin sheath and nodes of Ranvier
key_terms.definition: The insulating sheath formed by Schwann cells around a myelinated axon; the nodes of Ranvier are the gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths where the membrane is exposed.
The electrical potential difference across the plasma membrane of a resting neuron, with the outer surface positive and the inner surface negative (about −70 mV).

An active-transport pump in the axonal membrane that moves 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out of the cell for every 2 K<sup>+</sup> it moves in, using ATP, and so maintains the ionic gradients of the resting membrane.
The reversal of polarity of the membrane at a stimulated site when it becomes freely permeable to Na<sup>+</sup> and Na<sup>+</sup> rushes in, making the inside positive and the outside negative.
The electrical potential difference across the membrane at a depolarised site; it is the nerve impulse.
Restoration of the resting potential at an excited site when the short-lived Na<sup>+</sup> permeability is followed by a rise in K<sup>+</sup> permeability and K<sup>+</sup> diffuses out.
Conduction in a myelinated fibre in which the impulse jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next, making transmission much faster than in a non-myelinated fibre.
The junction between two neurons formed by the membranes of a pre-synaptic and a post-synaptic neuron, which may (chemical synapse) or may not (electrical synapse) be separated by a synaptic cleft.
A chemical stored in synaptic vesicles of the axon terminal that is released into the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the post-synaptic membrane to generate a new potential.
The three protective membranes covering the brain and spinal cord: the outer thick dura mater, the thin middle arachnoid, and the inner pia mater in contact with the brain tissue.
The folded layer of cells covering each cerebral hemisphere; grey matter containing motor, sensory and association areas.
The tract of nerve fibres connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres.
Regions of the cerebral cortex that are neither clearly sensory nor motor and are responsible for complex functions such as intersensory associations, memory and communication.

The inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres together with deep structures such as the amygdala and hippocampus; with the hypothalamus it regulates sexual behaviour, emotional reactions and motivation.
The four round swellings (lobes) that make up the dorsal portion of the midbrain.
The midbrain and the hindbrain (pons and medulla) together; it connects the forebrain to the spinal cord.
The entire process of response to a peripheral nervous stimulation that occurs involuntarily, without conscious effort or thought, and requires the involvement of a part of the CNS.
The pathway of a reflex: receptor → afferent neuron (through the dorsal root) → CNS → efferent neuron (through the ventral root) → effector.

formula_sheet.name: Divisions of the human neural system
formula_sheet.expr: Neural system → CNS (brain + spinal cord) and PNS (all nerves). PNS fibres: afferent (to CNS) and efferent (from CNS). PNS divisions: somatic (skeletal muscle, voluntary) and autonomic (involuntary organs) → sympathetic + parasympathetic
formula_sheet.note: 12 pairs of cranial nerves, 31 pairs of spinal nerves (numbers not in the rationalised text but asked in school papers).

formula_sheet.name: Neural organisation across animals
formula_sheet.expr: Hydra: network of neurons, no brain. Insects: brain + ganglia + neural tissues. Vertebrates: developed brain, spinal cord, nerves
formula_sheet.note: Quote the three in NCERT order for the 'neural system in animals' question.

formula_sheet.name: Parts of a neuron
formula_sheet.expr: Cell body (cytoplasm, organelles, Nissl's granules) · Dendrites (short, branched, Nissl's granules, carry impulse towards cell body) · Axon (long, branched end, synaptic knobs with synaptic vesicles of neurotransmitter, carries impulse away)
formula_sheet.note: Nissl's granules: cell body and dendrites only.

formula_sheet.name: Types of neurons by processes
formula_sheet.expr: Multipolar: 1 axon + 2 or more dendrites, cerebral cortex · Bipolar: 1 axon + 1 dendrite, retina of eye · Unipolar: cell body with one axon only, embryonic stage
formula_sheet.note: Location is the part that is tested.

formula_sheet.name: Myelinated versus non-myelinated axons
formula_sheet.expr: Myelinated: Schwann cells form myelin sheath, nodes of Ranvier between sheaths, spinal and cranial nerves, fast saltatory conduction · Non-myelinated: Schwann cell present but no sheath, autonomous and somatic neural systems, slower continuous conduction
formula_sheet.note: Both have Schwann cells; only one has a sheath.

formula_sheet.name: Ion distribution across the resting axonal membrane
formula_sheet.expr: Inside (axoplasm): high K<sup>+</sup>, high negatively charged proteins, low Na<sup>+</sup> · Outside: high Na<sup>+</sup>, low K<sup>+</sup> · Membrane: more permeable to K<sup>+</sup>, nearly impermeable to Na<sup>+</sup>, impermeable to the proteins
formula_sheet.note: Result: outside positive, inside negative = polarised = resting potential (about −70 mV, value not in NCERT).

formula_sheet.name: Sodium–potassium pump
formula_sheet.expr: 3 Na<sup>+</sup> pumped out for every 2 K<sup>+</sup> pumped in; active transport using ATP
formula_sheet.note: Maintains the ionic gradients; the net loss of one positive charge per cycle helps keep the inside negative.

formula_sheet.name: Generation and conduction of the impulse
formula_sheet.expr: Stimulus at A → freely permeable to Na<sup>+</sup> → Na<sup>+</sup> influx → inside +, outside − (depolarised) → action potential. Inner current A → B, outer current B → A → B depolarises → repeated along axon. Na<sup>+</sup> permeability short-lived → K<sup>+</sup> permeability rises → K<sup>+</sup> out → resting potential restored (repolarisation)
formula_sheet.note: Action potential = nerve impulse. All-or-none; one direction.

formula_sheet.name: Chemical synaptic transmission
formula_sheet.expr: Impulse at axon terminal → synaptic vesicles move to membrane → fuse, release neurotransmitter into cleft → bind specific receptors on post-synaptic membrane → ion channels open, ions enter → new potential (excitatory or inhibitory)
formula_sheet.note: Electrical synapse: membranes very close, current flows directly, faster, rare in our body.

formula_sheet.name: Meninges and coverings
formula_sheet.expr: Skull → dura mater (outer, thick) → arachnoid (thin, middle) → pia mater (inner, touches brain); cerebrospinal fluid between arachnoid and pia and in the ventricles

formula_sheet.name: Forebrain facts
formula_sheet.expr: Cerebrum: longitudinal fissure, two hemispheres, corpus callosum, cortex = grey matter (cell bodies) with motor, sensory, association areas; inner white matter (myelinated tracts) · Thalamus: coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling · Hypothalamus: eating, drinking, body temperature, neurosecretory cells (hormones), master clock · Limbic system: amygdala, hippocampus; sexual behaviour, emotions, motivation
formula_sheet.note: Most developed part of the brain: cerebrum.

formula_sheet.name: Midbrain and hindbrain facts
formula_sheet.expr: Midbrain: between thalamus/hypothalamus and pons; cerebral aqueduct passes through; dorsal corpora quadrigemina (four lobes) · Pons: fibre tracts interconnecting brain regions · Cerebellum: very convoluted surface for more neurons; balance and coordination of movement · Medulla: connected to spinal cord; respiration, cardiovascular reflexes, gastric secretions

formula_sheet.name: Reflex arc
formula_sheet.expr: Receptor → afferent (sensory) neuron, cell body in dorsal root ganglion, enters via dorsal root → spinal cord grey matter (interneuron) → efferent (motor) neuron leaves via ventral root → effector (muscle)
formula_sheet.note: At least one afferent and one efferent neuron in series; involuntary but involves the CNS. NCERT example: knee-jerk reflex.

diagrams.title: Structure of a neuron (NCERT Fig. 18.1)
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a star-shaped cell body with a large nucleus and dots for Nissl's granules, and several short branching dendrites projecting from it. From one side draw a single long axon; along the axon draw a series of sausage-shaped Schwann cells forming the myelin sheath, with small gaps between them, and at the far end branch the axon into three or four terminals each ending in a small bulb. At site A (depolarised) write minus signs on the outer surface and plus signs on the inner surface; at site B (resting) write plus signs outside and minus signs inside. Draw an arrow on the inner surface from A to B and an arrow on the outer surface from B to A to show the current loop, and a short arrow of Na<sup>+</sup> entering at A. Leave a narrow gap below it, the synaptic cleft, and below the gap draw the post-synaptic membrane with small receptor shapes on it. Show one vesicle fused with the pre-synaptic membrane releasing dots of neurotransmitter into the cleft and dots attached to the receptors. Inside the cerebrum draw the curved band of the corpus callosum; below it mark the thalamus and, at its base, the hypothalamus. diagrams.title: Reflex arc: the knee-jerk reflex (NCERT Fig. 18.5)

On one side draw the leg with the kneecap and the thigh muscle. diagrams.title: Myelinated and non-myelinated nerve fibres

In the upper (myelinated) axon draw a chain of Schwann cells wrapped in thick spirals around the axon with clear gaps between them, and label Schwann cell, myelin sheath, node of Ranvier, axon; add a dotted jumping arrow from node to node labelled saltatory conduction. In the lower (non-myelinated) axon draw Schwann cells simply resting on the axon without any wrapping, label Schwann cell and axon, and add a continuous arrow labelled continuous conduction. Bipolar: an elongated cell body with a single dendrite at one end and a single axon at the other; write 'retina of eye' below. Unipolar: a rounded cell body with a single process, the axon, emerging from it; write 'embryonic stage' below. Label cell body, dendrite and axon on each, and give each its name and location.
