diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a horizontal strip for the axonal membrane with 'outside' above and 'inside (axoplasm)' below. Above the membrane write 'Na<sup>+</sup> high, K<sup>+</sup> low' with a row of plus signs against the membrane; below write 'K<sup>+</sup> high, Na<sup>+</sup> low, proteins<sup>−</sup>' with a row of minus signs against the membrane. In the membrane draw a K<sup>+</sup> leak channel with a small arrow for K<sup>+</sup> going out, a closed Na<sup>+</sup> channel, and the sodium–potassium pump as a shaded oval with a thick arrow showing 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out and 2 K<sup>+</sup> in and 'ATP' written beside it. Label: axonal membrane, K<sup>+</sup> channel (open), Na<sup>+</sup> channel (closed), Na<sup>+</sup>–K<sup>+</sup> pump, resting potential (inside negative).

diagrams.title: Flow chart of the human neural system
diagrams.how_to_draw: Start with a box 'Human neural system' at the top. Branch into 'Central neural system (brain, spinal cord)' and 'Peripheral neural system (all nerves)'. Under the PNS branch into 'Afferent fibres (to CNS)' and 'Efferent fibres (from CNS)', and separately into 'Somatic neural system (skeletal muscles, voluntary)' and 'Autonomic neural system (involuntary organs)'. Under autonomic branch into 'Sympathetic' and 'Parasympathetic'. Under the CNS write 'Brain: forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain' and 'Spinal cord'. Keep every box to a name plus a two-word function.

ncert_questions.q: Briefly describe the structure of the brain.
ncert_questions.a:
The brain is the central information processing organ and the command and control system of the body. It is protected by the skull and covered by three cranial meninges: the outer thick dura mater, the very thin middle arachnoid, and the inner pia mater in contact with the brain tissue. It is divided into three major parts.

  1. Forebrain: consists of the cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus. The cerebrum is the largest part; a longitudinal fissure divides it into two cerebral hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum. Its outer layer, the cerebral cortex, is grey matter (concentration of cell bodies) containing motor, sensory and association areas; the inner region of myelinated tracts is white matter. The cerebrum wraps around the thalamus, a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling. The hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus and contains centres for eating, drinking and body temperature and groups of neurosecretory cells that secrete hormones. The inner parts of the hemispheres with the amygdala and hippocampus form the limbic system (emotions, sexual behaviour, motivation).
  2. Midbrain: located between the thalamus/hypothalamus and the pons. The cerebral aqueduct passes through it; its dorsal portion consists of four round swellings, the corpora quadrigemina.
  3. Hindbrain: consists of the pons (fibre tracts interconnecting different brain regions), the cerebellum (very convoluted surface for more neurons; balance and coordination of movement) and the medulla oblongata (connected to the spinal cord; centres for respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions).

The midbrain and hindbrain together form the brain stem, which continues as the spinal cord. (A labelled sagittal section, as in Fig. 18.4, should accompany this answer.)

ncert_questions.q: Compare the central neural system (CNS) and the peripheral neural system (PNS).
ncert_questions.a:
CNS: consists of the brain and the spinal cord; it is the site of information processing and control; it is protected by the skull and vertebral column and by the meninges; it contains both grey and white matter and the nerve cell bodies that integrate information.

PNS: comprises all the nerves of the body associated with the CNS (12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves); it carries information to the CNS through afferent fibres and from the CNS to tissues and organs through efferent fibres; it is divided into the somatic neural system (voluntary control of skeletal muscle) and the autonomic neural system (involuntary organs), the latter further divided into sympathetic and parasympathetic systems. The PNS does not process information; it only conducts it.

ncert_questions.q: Compare resting potential and action potential.
ncert_questions.a:
Resting potential: the potential difference across the membrane of a neuron that is not conducting an impulse. The membrane is more permeable to K+ and nearly impermeable to Na+; the Na+–K+ pump keeps Na+ high outside and K+ high inside; the outer surface is positive and the inner surface negative (polarised state, about −70 mV).

Action potential: the potential difference across the membrane at a site that has been stimulated. The membrane becomes freely permeable to Na+, Na+ rushes in and the polarity reverses, with the inner surface positive and the outer surface negative (depolarised state, about +30 mV). The action potential is the nerve impulse; it is short-lived and is followed by K+ efflux, which restores the resting potential.

ncert_questions.q: Explain the following processes: (a) polarisation of the membrane of a nerve fibre; (b) depolarisation of the membrane of a nerve fibre.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Polarisation. When a neuron is resting, its axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to K+ and nearly impermeable to Na+; it is also impermeable to the negatively charged proteins of the axoplasm. So the axoplasm contains a high concentration of K+ and negatively charged proteins and a low concentration of Na+, while the fluid outside has high Na+ and low K+. These gradients are maintained by the active transport of the sodium–potassium pump, which moves 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in. As a result the outer surface of the membrane is positively charged and the inner surface negatively charged; the membrane is polarised and the potential difference across it is the resting potential.

(b) Depolarisation. When a stimulus is applied at a site on the polarised membrane, the membrane at that site becomes freely permeable to Na+. There is a rapid influx of Na+, which reverses the polarity: the outer surface becomes negative and the inner surface positive. The membrane is now depolarised, and the potential difference across it at that site is the action potential, which is the nerve impulse.

ncert_questions.q: Explain the conduction of a nerve impulse along a nerve fibre.
ncert_questions.a: Let the membrane be depolarised at site A by a stimulus, so that at A the inner surface is positive and the outer surface negative, while at the neighbouring site B, which is still resting, the outer surface is positive and the inner surface negative. Because of this difference in polarity a current flows on the inner surface of the membrane from site A to site B and on the outer surface from site B to site A, completing a circuit of current flow. This local current reverses the polarity at site B, so an action potential is generated at B; the impulse generated at A has thus arrived at B. The sequence is repeated along the length of the axon and the impulse is conducted along the fibre. Meanwhile the short-lived rise in Na+ permeability at A is followed by a rise in K+ permeability; K+ diffuses out and the resting potential at A is restored, so the fibre is again ready for stimulation. In a myelinated fibre these events occur only at the nodes of Ranvier and the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), which is faster.

ncert_questions.q: Explain the transmission of a nerve impulse across a chemical synapse (mechanism of synaptic transmission).
ncert_questions.a:
A chemical synapse is formed by the membranes of a pre-synaptic neuron and a post-synaptic neuron separated by a fluid-filled synaptic cleft. The axon terminals of the pre-synaptic neuron contain synaptic vesicles filled with neurotransmitters. The steps are:

  1. When an impulse (action potential) arrives at the axon terminal, it stimulates the movement of the synaptic vesicles towards the pre-synaptic membrane.
  2. The vesicles fuse with the plasma membrane and release their neurotransmitters into the synaptic cleft.
  3. The released neurotransmitters diffuse across the cleft and bind to their specific receptors present on the post-synaptic membrane.
  4. This binding opens ion channels in the post-synaptic membrane, allowing the entry of ions which generate a new potential in the post-synaptic neuron.

The new potential may be excitatory or inhibitory depending on the ion channels opened. Transmission is one-way and slightly slower than at an electrical synapse. (Draw the labelled synapse of Fig. 18.3.)

ncert_questions.q: Draw labelled diagrams of (a) a neuron and (b) the brain.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Neuron: draw the cell body with nucleus and Nissl's granules, branching dendrites, a long axon covered by Schwann cells forming the myelin sheath with nodes of Ranvier between them, and branched axon terminals ending in synaptic knobs. Labels: dendrite, cell body, nucleus, Nissl's granules, axon, Schwann cell, myelin sheath, node of Ranvier, axon terminal.

(b) Brain (sagittal section): draw the convoluted cerebrum with the corpus callosum inside, the thalamus and hypothalamus below it, the midbrain with corpora quadrigemina and cerebral aqueduct, the pons, the cerebellum at the back and the medulla oblongata continuing into the spinal cord. Labels: cerebrum, corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, corpora quadrigemina, pons, cerebellum, medulla oblongata, spinal cord.

ncert_questions.q: Write a short note on neural coordination.
ncert_questions.a: Coordination is the process through which two or more organs interact and complement each other's functions. Neural coordination is the coordination provided by the neural system, which is made of highly specialised cells called neurons that can detect, receive and transmit stimuli. The neural system provides an organised network of point-to-point connections, so its coordination is rapid and precise. Sensory receptors detect a change, afferent neurons carry the information to the CNS (brain and spinal cord), the CNS processes it, and efferent neurons carry the command to effectors (muscles and glands), which respond. For example, during exercise the neural system raises the heart rate and the breathing rate and directs blood to the muscles. Neural coordination is supplemented by the slower chemical coordination of the endocrine system; the two meet in the hypothalamus.

ncert_questions.q: Write short notes on (b) forebrain, (c) midbrain and (d) hindbrain.
ncert_questions.a:
(b) Forebrain: consists of the cerebrum, thalamus and hypothalamus. The cerebrum, the largest part, is divided by the longitudinal fissure into two hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum; its cortex is grey matter with motor, sensory and association areas (intersensory associations, memory, communication), and its inner part is white matter. The thalamus is a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling. The hypothalamus, at the base of the thalamus, has centres for eating, drinking and body temperature and neurosecretory cells that secrete hormones. The inner hemispheres, amygdala and hippocampus form the limbic system, which regulates sexual behaviour, emotions and motivation.

(c) Midbrain: located between the thalamus/hypothalamus of the forebrain and the pons of the hindbrain. The cerebral aqueduct passes through it. Its dorsal portion consists of four round swellings called the corpora quadrigemina. With the hindbrain it forms the brain stem.

(d) Hindbrain: consists of the pons, cerebellum and medulla. The pons is made of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain. The cerebellum has a very convoluted surface that provides space for many more neurons; it maintains balance and coordinates voluntary movements. The medulla is connected to the spinal cord and contains centres controlling respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions.

ncert_questions.q: Write a short note on the synapse.
ncert_questions.a: A synapse is the junction through which a nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to another. It is formed by the membranes of a pre-synaptic neuron and a post-synaptic neuron, which may or may not be separated by a gap called the synaptic cleft. There are two types. At an electrical synapse the two membranes are in very close proximity and electrical current flows directly from one neuron to the other; transmission is faster, but such synapses are rare in our body. At a chemical synapse the membranes are separated by a fluid-filled synaptic cleft and transmission is carried out by neurotransmitters stored in synaptic vesicles of the axon terminal; on arrival of an impulse the vesicles release the neurotransmitter into the cleft, it binds to receptors on the post-synaptic membrane, ion channels open and a new potential (excitatory or inhibitory) is generated in the post-synaptic neuron.

ncert_questions.q: Explain the role of Na<sup>+</sup> in the generation of the action potential.
ncert_questions.a: In a resting neuron the membrane is nearly impermeable to Na+, and the sodium–potassium pump keeps the Na+ concentration high outside and low inside, which contributes to the polarised state (outside positive, inside negative). When a stimulus is applied at a site, the membrane there becomes freely permeable to Na+. Na+ rushes in along its concentration gradient. This rapid influx of positive charge reverses the polarity of the membrane, making the inner surface positive and the outer surface negative. The membrane is depolarised and the potential difference across it at that site is the action potential, i.e. the nerve impulse. Thus the entry of Na+ is the event that generates the action potential; the subsequent efflux of K+ ends it and restores the resting potential.

ncert_questions.q: Differentiate between (a) myelinated and non-myelinated axons; (b) dendrites and axons.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Myelinated axons are enveloped by Schwann cells that form a myelin sheath around the axon; the gaps between adjacent sheaths are the nodes of Ranvier; they are found in spinal and cranial nerves; conduction is saltatory (node to node) and fast. Non-myelinated axons are enclosed by a Schwann cell that does not form a myelin sheath; there are no nodes of Ranvier; they are commonly found in the autonomous and somatic neural systems; conduction is continuous and slower.

(b) Dendrites are short, numerous fibres that branch repeatedly, project out of the cell body, contain Nissl's granules and transmit impulses towards the cell body. The axon is a single long fibre, without Nissl's granules, whose distal end is branched into terminals with bulb-like synaptic knobs containing synaptic vesicles of neurotransmitter; it transmits impulses away from the cell body to a synapse or a neuro-muscular junction.

ncert_questions.q: Differentiate between (c) thalamus and hypothalamus; (d) cerebrum and cerebellum.
ncert_questions.a:
(c) The thalamus is the structure the cerebrum wraps around; it is a major coordinating (relay) centre for sensory and motor signalling. The hypothalamus lies at the base of the thalamus; it contains centres controlling the urge for eating and drinking and the body temperature, and groups of neurosecretory cells that secrete hormones; with the limbic system it regulates emotions, and it acts as the body's master clock.

(d) The cerebrum is part of the forebrain and is the largest and most developed part of the brain; it is divided into two hemispheres joined by the corpus callosum; its outer cortex is grey matter with motor, sensory and association areas responsible for intelligence, memory, communication and voluntary control. The cerebellum is part of the hindbrain, smaller, with a very convoluted surface to accommodate more neurons; it maintains balance and posture and coordinates voluntary movements.

ncert_questions.q: Answer the following: (a) Which part of the human brain is the most developed? (b) Which part of our central neural system acts as a master clock?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) The cerebrum, in particular its cerebral cortex, is the most developed part of the human brain; it is the seat of intelligence, memory, reasoning, speech and voluntary actions.

(b) The hypothalamus acts as the master clock; it controls the circadian rhythms of the body and, through its neurosecretory cells, links the neural and endocrine systems.

ncert_questions.q: Distinguish between (a) afferent neurons and efferent neurons; (b) impulse conduction in a myelinated nerve fibre and an unmyelinated nerve fibre; (c) cranial nerves and spinal nerves.
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Afferent (sensory) neurons carry impulses from tissues, organs and receptors to the CNS; in a reflex they enter the spinal cord through the dorsal root and their cell bodies lie in the dorsal root ganglion. Efferent (motor) neurons carry impulses from the CNS to effectors such as muscles and glands; they leave the spinal cord through the ventral root and their cell bodies lie in the grey matter of the CNS.

(b) In a myelinated fibre the myelin sheath insulates the axon, so depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier and the impulse jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction); conduction is fast. In an unmyelinated fibre there is no sheath, every part of the membrane is depolarised in turn (continuous conduction) and conduction is slow.

(c) Cranial nerves arise from the brain, are 12 pairs, and may be sensory, motor or mixed. Spinal nerves arise from the spinal cord, are 31 pairs, and are all mixed, each formed by a dorsal (sensory) and a ventral (motor) root.

pyq.q: Nissl's granules are found in the
options: Myelin sheath and nodes of Ranvier
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: NCERT states that the cell body contains Nissl's granules and that the dendrites also contain them. The axon lacks them.

pyq.q: The sodium–potassium pump in the axonal membrane transports
options: Equal numbers of Na<sup>+</sup> and K<sup>+</sup> in opposite directions
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: The pump moves 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out of the cell for every 2 K<sup>+</sup> it brings in, by active transport, and thereby maintains the ionic gradients of the resting membrane.

pyq.q: Bipolar neurons are found in the
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Bipolar neurons (one axon, one dendrite) occur in the retina; multipolar neurons are in the cerebral cortex and unipolar neurons are usually found in the embryonic stage.

pyq.q: Corpora quadrigemina is a part of the
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: The dorsal portion of the midbrain consists of four round swellings called the corpora quadrigemina.

pyq.q: During the resting state the axonal membrane is
options: More permeable to Na<sup>+</sup> and nearly impermeable to K<sup>+</sup>
More permeable to K<sup>+</sup> and nearly impermeable to Na<sup>+</sup>
Equally permeable to Na<sup>+</sup> and K<sup>+</sup>
Impermeable to both Na<sup>+</sup> and K<sup>+</sup>
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: A resting axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to K<sup>+</sup> and nearly impermeable to Na<sup>+</sup>; it is also impermeable to the negatively charged proteins of the axoplasm.

pyq.q: The centres that control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions are located in the
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: NCERT lists respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions as the functions controlled by centres in the medulla, which is connected to the spinal cord.

pyq.q: The gaps between two adjacent myelin sheaths on an axon are called
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: In a myelinated fibre the Schwann cells form the myelin sheath and the gaps between adjacent sheaths are the nodes of Ranvier, where the impulse jumps during saltatory conduction.

pyq.q: Which of the following correctly lists the meninges from the outside inwards?
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The outer thick layer is the dura mater, the very thin middle layer is the arachnoid, and the inner layer in contact with the brain tissue is the pia mater.

pyq.q: Neurotransmitters are stored in
options: Nissl's granules of the cell body
Synaptic vesicles of the axon terminal
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Each axon branch ends in a synaptic knob that possesses synaptic vesicles containing neurotransmitters; these are released into the cleft when an impulse arrives.

pyq.q: Impulse transmission across an electrical synapse is
options: Slower than across a chemical synapse and common in humans
Faster than across a chemical synapse and common in humans
Faster than across a chemical synapse and rare in humans
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: At an electrical synapse current flows directly from one neuron to the next, so transmission is always faster than at a chemical synapse, but such synapses are rare in our system.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Impulse conduction is faster in a myelinated nerve fibre than in a non-myelinated fibre. Reason (R): In a myelinated fibre depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier, so the impulse jumps from node to node.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The myelin sheath insulates the axon; the membrane is exposed only at the nodes, so the action potential jumps from node to node (saltatory conduction), which is exactly why myelinated fibres conduct faster.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The cerebral cortex is called grey matter. Reason (R): The cerebral cortex has a high concentration of neuron cell bodies.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: NCERT: the cortex is referred to as grey matter due to its greyish appearance, which is due to the concentration of neuron cell bodies; the inner myelinated tracts form the white matter.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Electrical synapses are the common type of synapse in the human neural system. Reason (R): At an electrical synapse the electrical current flows directly from the pre-synaptic neuron to the post-synaptic neuron.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Electrical synapses are rare in our system, so A is false. R correctly describes how an electrical synapse works, so R is true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Reflex action is an involuntary response. Reason (R): Reflex action does not involve any part of the central neural system.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: A reflex is involuntary, but by definition it requires the involvement of a part of the CNS, usually the spinal cord, where the afferent neuron connects to the efferent neuron. So R is false.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): In a resting neuron the inner surface of the axonal membrane is negatively charged. Reason (R): The resting membrane is nearly impermeable to Na<sup>+</sup>, more permeable to K<sup>+</sup>, and impermeable to the negatively charged proteins of the axoplasm, while the Na<sup>+</sup>–K<sup>+</sup> pump moves 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out for 2 K<sup>+</sup> in.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The trapped negative proteins, the outward leak of K<sup>+</sup> and the 3:2 pump together leave the inside negative and the outside positive, which is the polarised resting state; R explains A.

pyq.q: Define a synapse. Name its two types.
pyq.answer:
A synapse is the junction between two neurons through which a nerve impulse is transmitted from one neuron to the next. It is formed by the membranes of a pre-synaptic neuron and a post-synaptic neuron, which may or may not be separated by a gap called the synaptic cleft. (1 mark)

The two types are the electrical synapse (membranes in very close proximity, current flows directly, faster but rare) and the chemical synapse (membranes separated by a synaptic cleft, transmission by neurotransmitters). (1 mark)

pyq.q: Name the three meninges covering the human brain in order from outside to inside, and state which of them is in contact with the brain tissue.
pyq.answer:
From outside inwards: the dura mater (outer thick layer), the arachnoid (very thin middle layer) and the pia mater (inner layer). (1½ marks)

The pia mater is in contact with the brain tissue. (½ mark)

pyq.q: What is the difference between afferent and efferent nerve fibres? Give one example of each.
pyq.answer:
Afferent fibres transmit impulses from tissues and organs (receptors) to the CNS; example: the sensory neuron of the knee-jerk reflex, which carries the impulse from the muscle spindle through the dorsal root into the spinal cord. (1 mark)

Efferent fibres transmit regulatory impulses from the CNS to the concerned peripheral tissues and organs (effectors); example: the motor neuron of the same reflex, which leaves through the ventral root and makes the thigh muscle contract. (1 mark)

pyq.q: State two functions of the hypothalamus.
pyq.answer: Any two: (i) it contains centres which control the urge for eating and drinking; (ii) it contains the centre for regulation of body temperature; (iii) it contains groups of neurosecretory cells that secrete hormones and thereby links the neural and endocrine systems; (iv) along with the limbic system it regulates sexual behaviour, emotional reactions and motivation; (v) it acts as the master clock controlling circadian rhythms. (1 mark each)

pyq.q: What is a reflex action? Give one example.
pyq.answer:
A reflex action is the entire process of response to a peripheral nervous stimulation that occurs involuntarily, i.e. without conscious effort or thought, and requires the involvement of a part of the central neural system (usually the spinal cord). (1½ marks)

Example: the knee-jerk reflex, or the sudden withdrawal of the hand on touching a hot object. (½ mark)

pyq.q: Why is the cerebral cortex grey while the inner part of the cerebrum is white?
pyq.answer:
The cerebral cortex is grey because it contains a high concentration of the cell bodies of neurons, which gives it a greyish appearance (grey matter). (1 mark)

The inner part of the cerebral hemisphere is made of fibre tracts covered by myelin sheaths, which give it an opaque white appearance (white matter). (1 mark)

pyq.q: Describe the three types of neurons on the basis of the number of axons and dendrites, giving the location of each.
pyq.answer:
Based on the number of axons and dendrites, neurons are of three types:

  1. Multipolar neurons have one axon and two or more dendrites; they are found in the cerebral cortex. (1 mark)
  2. Bipolar neurons have one axon and one dendrite; they are found in the retina of the eye. (1 mark)
  3. Unipolar neurons have a cell body with one axon only; they are usually found in the embryonic stage. (1 mark)

(A small sketch of the three types earns the label marks if the question says 'with diagrams'.)

pyq.q: Differentiate between a chemical synapse and an electrical synapse on three points.
pyq.answer:
• Gap: at a chemical synapse the pre- and post-synaptic membranes are separated by a fluid-filled synaptic cleft; at an electrical synapse the membranes are in very close proximity with no real gap. (1 mark)
  • Mode of transmission: a chemical synapse transmits through neurotransmitters released from synaptic vesicles that bind to receptors on the post-synaptic membrane; at an electrical synapse the electrical current flows directly from one neuron into the other, like conduction along a single axon. (1 mark)
  • Speed and occurrence: transmission across a chemical synapse is slower (synaptic delay) and chemical synapses are the common type in our body; transmission across an electrical synapse is always faster, but electrical synapses are rare in our system. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Explain the role of the sodium–potassium pump and the selective permeability of the membrane in maintaining the resting potential of a neuron.
pyq.answer:
The axonal membrane at rest is comparatively more permeable to K+, nearly impermeable to Na+, and impermeable to the negatively charged proteins present in the axoplasm. (1 mark)

Consequently the axoplasm has a high concentration of K+ and negatively charged proteins and a low concentration of Na+, whereas the fluid outside has a low concentration of K+ and a high concentration of Na+. K+ leaks outwards through its channels, leaving the negative proteins inside. (1 mark)

These concentration gradients would dissipate by diffusion, but they are maintained by the active transport of ions by the sodium–potassium pump, which transports 3 Na+ outwards for every 2 K+ into the cell using ATP. The result is that the outer surface of the membrane is positively charged and the inner surface negatively charged, i.e. the membrane is polarised, and this potential difference is the resting potential. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Name the parts of the hindbrain and give one function of each.
pyq.answer:
The hindbrain comprises the pons, the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata.

  • Pons: consists of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain (it bridges the cerebellum, the cerebrum and the medulla, and helps regulate breathing). (1 mark)
  • Cerebellum: has a very convoluted surface providing space for many more neurons; it maintains balance and posture and coordinates voluntary movements. (1 mark)
  • Medulla oblongata: is connected to the spinal cord and contains centres that control respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Draw a flow chart showing the divisions of the human neural system.
pyq.answer:
Human neural system → (i) Central neural system: brain (forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain) and spinal cord; (ii) Peripheral neural system: all the nerves associated with the CNS. (1 mark)

PNS nerve fibres → afferent fibres (tissues/organs → CNS) and efferent fibres (CNS → tissues/organs). (1 mark)

PNS divisions → somatic neural system (CNS → skeletal muscles, voluntary) and autonomic neural system (CNS → involuntary organs and smooth muscles) → sympathetic neural system and parasympathetic neural system. (1 mark)

(Present as boxes and arrows in the exam.)

pyq.q: With the help of a labelled diagram, explain how a nerve impulse is generated and conducted along a nerve fibre.
pyq.answer:
Diagram: draw an axon showing site A (depolarised: outside −, inside +) and site B (resting: outside +, inside −) with the current arrows, inner surface A → B and outer surface B → A (Fig. 18.2). (1 mark)

Resting (polarised) membrane: the axonal membrane at rest is more permeable to K+ and nearly impermeable to Na+; K+ and negatively charged proteins are high inside and Na+ is high outside; the Na+–K+ pump (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in) maintains these gradients; the outer surface is positive and the inner surface negative, giving the resting potential. (1 mark)

Generation (depolarisation): when a stimulus is applied at site A the membrane there becomes freely permeable to Na+; Na+ rushes in and reverses the polarity, making the inside positive and the outside negative; the membrane is depolarised and the potential difference at A is the action potential, i.e. the nerve impulse. (1 mark)

Conduction: at the adjacent site B the outer surface is still positive and the inner surface negative, so a current flows on the inner surface from A to B and on the outer surface from B to A, completing the circuit; this reverses the polarity at B and an action potential is generated at B. The sequence repeats along the axon and the impulse is conducted. (1 mark)

Repolarisation: the rise in Na+ permeability is extremely short-lived and is quickly followed by a rise in K+ permeability; K+ diffuses out and restores the resting potential at A, so the fibre is again responsive. In myelinated fibres this occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier and the impulse jumps from node to node, which is faster. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Draw a labelled diagram of a sagittal section of the human brain and describe the functions of the forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.
pyq.answer:
Diagram (Fig. 18.4) with labels: cerebrum, corpus callosum, thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain, corpora quadrigemina, pons, cerebellum, medulla oblongata, spinal cord. (2 marks)

Forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus): the cerebrum, with its cortex of grey matter containing motor, sensory and association areas, controls voluntary movements and is the seat of intelligence, memory, communication, speech and thought; the thalamus is a major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling; the hypothalamus controls the urge for eating and drinking and body temperature and secretes hormones through its neurosecretory cells; with the limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus) it regulates sexual behaviour, emotions and motivation. (1 mark)

Midbrain: lies between the forebrain and the pons; the cerebral aqueduct passes through it; its dorsal portion bears the corpora quadrigemina, four round swellings concerned with visual and auditory reflexes; it is part of the brain stem, relaying signals between forebrain and hindbrain. (1 mark)

Hindbrain (pons, cerebellum, medulla): the pons consists of fibre tracts that interconnect different regions of the brain; the cerebellum, with its highly convoluted surface, maintains balance and posture and coordinates voluntary movement; the medulla oblongata, connected to the spinal cord, contains centres controlling respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions. (1 mark)

pyq.q: What is a reflex arc? Describe the knee-jerk reflex with a labelled diagram, naming the components of the reflex arc in sequence.
pyq.answer:
Reflex arc: the pathway taken by an impulse during a reflex action, from the receptor to the effector through the CNS. It comprises at least one afferent neuron (receptor) and one efferent neuron (effector or excitor) appropriately arranged in a series; the stimulus and the response form the reflex arc. (1 mark)

Diagram (Fig. 18.5): cross-section of the spinal cord with grey and white matter, the receptor in the thigh muscle, the sensory neuron entering through the dorsal root with its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion, the interneuron in the grey matter, the motor neuron leaving through the ventral root, and the effector muscle. (2 marks)

Sequence in the knee jerk: (1) a tap below the kneecap stretches the thigh muscle; the stretch receptor (muscle spindle) generates impulses (stimulus and receptor); (2) the afferent (sensory) neuron carries the impulse through the dorsal nerve root into the spinal cord, its cell body lying in the dorsal root ganglion; (3) inside the grey matter the impulse is passed, directly or through an interneuron, to the efferent (motor) neuron; (4) the efferent neuron carries the impulse out through the ventral root to the effector, the thigh muscle; (5) the muscle contracts and the lower leg kicks forward, the response. (1½ marks)

Significance: because the pathway is short and does not wait for the brain, the response is rapid and protective; the brain is informed afterwards. (½ mark)

pyq.q: Draw a labelled diagram of a neuron. Describe the structure of a neuron and distinguish between myelinated and non-myelinated nerve fibres.
pyq.answer:
Diagram (Fig. 18.1) with labels: dendrite, cell body, nucleus, Nissl's granules, axon, Schwann cell, myelin sheath, node of Ranvier, axon terminal (synaptic knob). (1½ marks)

Structure: a neuron has three major parts. The cell body contains cytoplasm with typical cell organelles and, in addition, granular bodies called Nissl's granules. Dendrites are short fibres that branch repeatedly and project out of the cell body; they also contain Nissl's granules and transmit impulses towards the cell body. The axon is a long fibre whose distal end is branched; each branch terminates as a bulb-like synaptic knob possessing synaptic vesicles that contain neurotransmitters; axons transmit impulses away from the cell body to a synapse or a neuro-muscular junction. Based on the number of axons and dendrites, neurons are multipolar (cerebral cortex), bipolar (retina) or unipolar (embryonic stage). (2 marks)

Myelinated versus non-myelinated fibres: myelinated fibres are enveloped by Schwann cells that form a myelin sheath around the axon, with nodes of Ranvier between adjacent sheaths; they are found in spinal and cranial nerves and conduct impulses rapidly by saltatory conduction. Non-myelinated fibres are enclosed by a Schwann cell that does not form a myelin sheath, have no nodes of Ranvier, are commonly found in the autonomous and somatic neural systems, and conduct more slowly. (1½ marks)

pyq.q:
A doctor taps the tendon just below a patient's kneecap with a small hammer and the lower leg kicks forward without the patient trying to move it. The tap stretches the thigh muscle; a stretch receptor in the muscle sends an impulse along a sensory neuron into the spinal cord, where it is passed to a motor neuron that makes the same muscle contract.
(i) What kind of action is the knee jerk? Define it.
(ii) Through which root does the sensory neuron enter the spinal cord, and where is its cell body located?
(iii) Name the effector in this reflex and the root through which the motor neuron leaves the spinal cord.
(iv) Why does the leg move before the patient is aware of the tap?
pyq.answer:
(i) It is a reflex action: the process of response to a peripheral nervous stimulation that occurs involuntarily, without conscious effort or thought, and requires the involvement of a part of the CNS (here the spinal cord). (1 mark)

(ii) The sensory (afferent) neuron enters through the dorsal nerve root; its cell body lies in the dorsal root ganglion. (1 mark)

(iii) The effector is the thigh (extensor) muscle; the motor (efferent) neuron leaves through the ventral root. (1 mark)

(iv) The reflex arc is completed within the spinal cord (receptor → afferent neuron → spinal cord → efferent neuron → effector) without waiting for the brain to process the information; the impulse informing the brain travels separately and reaches consciousness only after the response has begun. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
A dentist injects a local anaesthetic near a nerve before drilling a tooth. The drug blocks the voltage-gated Na+ channels in the axonal membrane of the sensory nerve fibres, so that even when the tooth is stimulated the fibre does not become permeable to Na+. The patient feels no pain from the tooth, although the rest of the body is unaffected.
(i) State the condition of the axonal membrane in an unstimulated nerve fibre with respect to Na+ and K+.
(ii) What normally happens at a stimulated site to generate an action potential?
(iii) Explain why blocking Na+ channels prevents the sensation of pain.
(iv) Would the anaesthetic affect the resting potential of the fibre? Give a reason.
pyq.answer:
(i) In a resting fibre the axonal membrane is comparatively more permeable to K+ and nearly impermeable to Na+; Na+ is high outside and K+ high inside, maintained by the Na+–K+ pump, so the outside is positive and the inside negative (polarised, resting potential). (1 mark)

(ii) At a stimulated site the membrane becomes freely permeable to Na+; Na+ rushes in and reverses the polarity (inside positive, outside negative), i.e. the membrane is depolarised and an action potential is generated. (1 mark)

(iii) With the Na+ channels blocked the membrane cannot become permeable to Na+ when stimulated, so no depolarisation and no action potential occur; no impulse is generated or conducted along the sensory fibre to the CNS, hence no pain is perceived. (1 mark)

(iv) Essentially no. The resting potential depends on the K+ permeability, the trapped negative proteins and the Na+–K+ pump, not on the stimulus-gated Na+ channels, which are closed at rest anyway; the fibre stays polarised but cannot fire. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
A cyclist falls and injures the back of the head. In hospital he is found to be conscious and able to think and speak, but he cannot stand without swaying, his movements are clumsy and uncoordinated, and his breathing and heart rate are irregular.
(i) Which two parts of the brain are most likely affected? Name the region of the brain to which each belongs.
(ii) Explain the loss of balance and coordination.
(iii) Explain the irregular breathing and heart rate.
(iv) Why are his speech, thinking and memory unaffected?
pyq.answer:
(i) The cerebellum and the medulla oblongata; both belong to the hindbrain (the medulla is also part of the brain stem). (1 mark)

(ii) The cerebellum maintains balance and posture and coordinates voluntary movements; damage to it leaves the person able to move but unable to keep his balance or move smoothly. (1 mark)

(iii) The medulla contains the centres that control respiration and cardiovascular reflexes (and gastric secretions); injury to it disturbs the rhythm of breathing and the regulation of heart rate and blood pressure. (1 mark)

(iv) Speech, thinking, memory and consciousness are functions of the cerebrum (cerebral cortex with its association areas) in the forebrain, at the front and top of the skull, which was not injured in a blow to the back of the head. (1 mark)

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following animals has a neural system consisting of a simple network of neurons without a brain?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT gives Hydra as the animal with a network of neurons; insects have a brain with ganglia and vertebrates have a developed neural system.

practice_mcq.q: Multipolar neurons, with one axon and two or more dendrites, are found in the
practice_mcq.explanation: Multipolar neurons occur in the cerebral cortex; bipolar in the retina; unipolar usually in the embryonic stage.

practice_mcq.q: Non-myelinated nerve fibres are commonly found in the
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: unmyelinated fibres are commonly found in the autonomous and somatic neural systems, whereas myelinated fibres are found in spinal and cranial nerves.

practice_mcq.q: The axoplasm of a resting neuron contains
options: High K<sup>+</sup> and negatively charged proteins, low Na<sup>+</sup>
practice_mcq.explanation: Because the membrane is nearly impermeable to Na<sup>+</sup> and impermeable to the negative proteins, and the pump exports Na<sup>+</sup>, the inside is rich in K<sup>+</sup> and proteins and poor in Na<sup>+</sup>.

practice_mcq.q: Depolarisation of the axonal membrane at a stimulated site is caused by
practice_mcq.explanation: The stimulated membrane becomes freely permeable to Na<sup>+</sup>; the influx of Na<sup>+</sup> reverses the polarity, making the inside positive.

practice_mcq.q: The resting potential at the site of excitation is restored mainly by
options: Diffusion of K<sup>+</sup> out of the axon
practice_mcq.explanation: The short-lived rise in Na<sup>+</sup> permeability is followed by a rise in K<sup>+</sup> permeability; K<sup>+</sup> diffuses out and restores the resting potential (repolarisation).

practice_mcq.q: During conduction of an impulse, at the depolarised site A the current on the inner surface of the membrane flows
options: From site B to site A
From site A to site B
Not at all; only ions move
practice_mcq.explanation: The inside of A is positive and the inside of B is negative, so on the inner surface current flows from A to B, while on the outer surface it flows from B to A.

practice_mcq.q: Which statement about a chemical synapse is correct?
options: Pre- and post-synaptic membranes are in direct contact
Neurotransmitters are stored in the post-synaptic neuron
Neurotransmitters bind to specific receptors on the post-synaptic membrane
Transmission is faster than at an electrical synapse
practice_mcq.explanation: At a chemical synapse the membranes are separated by a cleft; the pre-synaptic vesicles release the neurotransmitter, which binds to receptors on the post-synaptic membrane and opens ion channels.

practice_mcq.q: The two cerebral hemispheres are connected by the
practice_mcq.explanation: The corpus callosum is a tract of nerve fibres connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres.

practice_mcq.q: Association areas of the cerebral cortex are responsible for
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT describes the association areas as regions neither clearly sensory nor motor, responsible for complex functions like intersensory associations, memory and communication.

practice_mcq.q: The major coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling that the cerebrum wraps around is the
practice_mcq.explanation: The thalamus is the coordinating centre for sensory and motor signalling; the hypothalamus lies at its base.

practice_mcq.q: The amygdala and hippocampus are parts of the
practice_mcq.explanation: The inner parts of the cerebral hemispheres with deep structures like the amygdala and hippocampus form the limbic lobe or limbic system, which with the hypothalamus regulates emotions, sexual behaviour and motivation.

practice_mcq.q: The cerebral aqueduct passes through the
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: a canal called the cerebral aqueduct passes through the midbrain.

practice_mcq.q: The part of the brain with a very convoluted surface that provides space for many more neurons and controls balance is the
practice_mcq.explanation: The cerebellum has a very convoluted surface to accommodate many more neurons and coordinates movement and balance.

practice_mcq.q: The brain stem is formed by the
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: the midbrain and hindbrain (pons and medulla) form the brain stem.

practice_mcq.q: The centres controlling the urge for eating and drinking and body temperature are located in the
practice_mcq.explanation: The hypothalamus contains these centres and also the neurosecretory cells that secrete hormones.

practice_mcq.q: In a reflex arc, the afferent neuron transmits the impulse into the spinal cord through the
practice_mcq.explanation: The afferent (sensory) neuron enters through the dorsal root, with its cell body in the dorsal root ganglion; the efferent neuron leaves through the ventral root.

practice_mcq.q: A reflex pathway must contain at least
options: One afferent and one efferent neuron in series
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT: the reflex pathway comprises at least one afferent neuron (receptor) and one efferent neuron (effector or excitor) appropriately arranged in a series.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is NOT a part of the forebrain?
practice_mcq.explanation: The pons is part of the hindbrain, together with the cerebellum and the medulla.

common_mistakes: Reversing the Na<sup>+</sup>–K<sup>+</sup> pump ratio. It is 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out for 2 K<sup>+</sup> in. Writing 2 out and 3 in, or the right numbers with the wrong directions, is marked wrong even if the rest of the answer is fine.

Saying the resting membrane is permeable to Na<sup>+</sup>. At rest it is more permeable to K<sup>+</sup> and nearly impermeable to Na<sup>+</sup>; Na<sup>+</sup> permeability rises only when a stimulus arrives. Students who swap the two ions lose the whole polarisation explanation.

Writing that the impulse 'crosses' or 'jumps' the synaptic cleft. At a chemical synapse the impulse ends at the pre-synaptic knob; the neurotransmitter crosses the cleft and a new potential is generated in the post-synaptic neuron. Only at an electrical synapse does current flow directly.
Placing Nissl's granules in the axon, or omitting them from the dendrites. They are in the cell body and the dendrites, not in the axon. Diagrams that dot the axon with granules are penalised.

Mixing the parts of the brain: putting the corpora quadrigemina in the hindbrain, the pons in the midbrain, or the hypothalamus outside the forebrain. Learn the three lists: forebrain (cerebrum, thalamus, hypothalamus), midbrain (cerebral aqueduct, corpora quadrigemina), hindbrain (pons, cerebellum, medulla).
Naming the meninges in the wrong order or spelling them loosely. Dura mater (outer), arachnoid (middle), pia mater (inner, touching the brain). The order is what the MCQ tests.

Drawing the reflex arc with the sensory neuron entering through the ventral root, or forgetting the dorsal root ganglion. Sensory in through the dorsal root with its cell body in the ganglion; motor out through the ventral root with its cell body in the grey matter.

Writing 'reflex action does not involve the CNS'. It is involuntary and does not involve conscious thought, but by NCERT's definition it requires the involvement of a part of the CNS, usually the spinal cord.

Giving 'controls involuntary functions' as the function of the medulla or 'controls the body' for the cerebrum. Examiners want the specific NCERT words: respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions for the medulla; motor, sensory and association areas, memory, communication for the cerebral cortex.
Confusing the somatic neural system (division of the PNS controlling skeletal muscle) with the sympathetic neural system (division of the autonomic system). A flow chart in the answer avoids this.
strategy:
This chapter is short in the rationalised book (five sections and five figures) but dense in examinable sentences, so the best preparation is to learn NCERT's own wording rather than a coaching summary. Spend the first sitting on the neuron and the impulse. Draw the neuron from memory with all nine labels, then write the polarisation, depolarisation, conduction and repolarisation as four numbered blocks with the site A/site B diagram. Say the pump ratio aloud, 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, until it is automatic. Then do the synapse: the one-sentence definition, the four steps of chemical transmission, and the three-point contrast with the electrical synapse.

Spend the second sitting on the brain. Learn the three lists (forebrain, midbrain, hindbrain parts) and attach one NCERT function to every name: thalamus coordinates sensory and motor signalling, hypothalamus controls eating, drinking and temperature and secretes hormones, cerebral aqueduct and corpora quadrigemina for the midbrain, pons is fibre tracts, cerebellum is balance with a convoluted surface, medulla is respiration, cardiovascular reflexes and gastric secretions. Draw the sagittal section twice. Finish with the reflex arc: draw the knee-jerk figure with the dorsal and ventral roots the right way round and write the sequence receptor → afferent → CNS → efferent → effector.

Memorise: the divisions flow chart, the three neuron types with locations, the ion distribution table, the meninges in order, and the named comparisons (dendrite/axon, thalamus/hypothalamus, cerebrum/cerebellum, afferent/efferent, cranial/spinal, myelinated/non-myelinated). Practise explaining, not memorising, the mechanism of impulse generation and synaptic transmission, because those are the 5-markers and the marking scheme rewards the sequence of events with the reason for each. In the exam give every 5-mark answer a labelled diagram; in this chapter the diagram is usually worth a third of the marks. Allow about 25 minutes for this chapter's questions in a three-hour paper.
revision_checklist: I can define coordination and contrast neural (point-to-point, fast) with endocrine (hormonal, slower) coordination, and quote Hydra, insects and vertebrates as the three levels of neural organisation.
I can draw the flow chart: CNS (brain, spinal cord) and PNS; afferent and efferent fibres; somatic and autonomic; sympathetic and parasympathetic; and define the visceral nervous system.

I can draw a neuron with nine labels and state that Nissl's granules are in the cell body and dendrites, that dendrites carry impulses towards and axons away from the cell body, and that synaptic knobs hold vesicles of neurotransmitter.
I know the three neuron types with their locations: multipolar (cerebral cortex), bipolar (retina), unipolar (embryonic stage).
I can distinguish myelinated (Schwann cells form a sheath, nodes of Ranvier, spinal and cranial nerves, saltatory) from non-myelinated fibres (no sheath, autonomous and somatic systems, slower).

I can state the resting membrane's permeabilities (more to K<sup>+</sup>, nearly none to Na<sup>+</sup>, none to negative proteins), the ion distribution inside and outside, and the pump ratio 3 Na<sup>+</sup> out : 2 K<sup>+</sup> in.

I can explain depolarisation (Na<sup>+</sup> influx, inside positive), the current loop between site A and site B (inner A → B, outer B → A), and repolarisation (K<sup>+</sup> efflux), with the NCERT diagram.
I can define a synapse, contrast electrical and chemical synapses, and write the four steps of chemical transmission ending with an excitatory or inhibitory potential.
I can list what the brain controls and name the skull and the three meninges in order: dura mater, arachnoid, pia mater.

I know the forebrain: cerebrum (longitudinal fissure, hemispheres, corpus callosum, grey cortex with motor, sensory and association areas, white matter inside), thalamus, hypothalamus (eating, drinking, temperature, neurosecretory cells) and the limbic system (amygdala, hippocampus; emotions, sexual behaviour, motivation).
I know the midbrain (between forebrain and pons; cerebral aqueduct; dorsal corpora quadrigemina) and that midbrain plus hindbrain form the brain stem.
I know the hindbrain: pons (fibre tracts), cerebellum (convoluted surface, balance and coordination), medulla (respiration, cardiovascular reflexes, gastric secretions).
I can answer: most developed part of the brain = cerebrum; master clock = hypothalamus; 12 pairs of cranial and 31 pairs of spinal nerves.

I can define reflex action with all three parts (peripheral stimulus, involuntary, involves the CNS), draw the knee-jerk reflex arc with the dorsal root ganglion and ventral root correctly placed, and write the sequence receptor → afferent → CNS → efferent → effector.
I have written the five named comparisons (dendrite/axon, thalamus/hypothalamus, cerebrum/cerebellum, afferent/efferent, cranial/spinal) as two-column tables at least once.
